subject: Art & Design
title: Display and Decorative Type
description: Learn Display and Decorative Type in one minute.

hook.text: A horror movie poster in Comic Sans? The font would kill the mood before the movie does.

buildup.text: Display fonts are designed for large sizes: headlines, logos, posters. Never for body text.

discovery.text: Script, blackletter, slab-serif, hand-drawn — display types carry extreme personality per letter.

twist.text: The more personality a font has, the faster it becomes annoying. Display fonts have a short shelf life.

climax.text: Use one display font for headlines and pair it with a neutral sans-serif for body. That's the formula.

punchline.text: Display fonts are spices. A pinch adds flavor. A cup ruins the dish.

quiz.question: Why should display fonts not be used for body text?
options: Their strong personality becomes tiring and reduces readability

details.summary: Display and decorative typefaces are designed for large sizes — headlines, posters, logos — rather than body text. They prioritize visual impact over extended readability: brush scripts, ornate serifs, geometric experiments.
details.whyItMatters: Display type is where typography becomes art. While body text must be invisible, display type is meant to be seen, commanding attention and establishing personality. It's the typographic equivalent of a building's facade.
takeaways: Display type is designed for large sizes and visual impact
It prioritizes personality and attention over readability
Display faces should never be used for body text

faq.question: How small can display type be used?
faq.answer: Most display typefaces work well at 24pt and above. Below that, their decorative details can become illegible or muddy. Test your specific display face at the intended size — some geometric display faces remain clear at 18pt, while ornate scripts may need 36pt or larger to be legible.

faq.question: How do you choose an appropriate display typeface?
faq.answer: Match the typeface's personality to the project's tone. A luxury brand wants elegant, refined characters. A children's brand wants playful, rounded forms. A tech startup wants geometric precision.
